summary: Surveys the state of IPv6 deployment as of 2022. It looks at how widely it is used, discusses remaining challenges, and suggests areas that need further investigation. It obsoletes RFC 6036.

eli5.summary: A progress report on how many people have switched to the newer internet address system, and what still gets in the way.

questions: what are the challenges of ipv6 adoption
what is ipv4 as a service
subtitle: A 2022 progress report on who has moved to IPv6, how, and what still holds the rest back.

tldr.problem: More than ten years after RFC 6036, nobody had an up-to-date picture of how far the move from IPv4 to IPv6 had actually got, or what was still in the way.
tldr.mechanism: The document gathers 2022 measurements of IPv6 users, websites and allocations, adds two operator and enterprise polls, describes five deployment scenarios, and lists common challenges.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 6036 and is informational only: it sets no protocol rules and mainly points to areas that still need investigation.

today: RFC 9386 is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 6036, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. Its numbers describe 2022, so they are a snapshot rather than the current state.

sections.title: Why a New Status Report
sections.content:
RFC 6036 recorded the IPv6 plans of a group of Internet Service Providers (ISPs) that answered a questionnaire in early 2010. RFC 9386 revisits the topic after more than ten years and obsoletes that document.

It gives three reasons for doing so. In some areas the lack of IPv4 addresses pushed carriers and content providers to IPv6. Some governments encouraged or enforced adoption. And global adoption seems to have reached a threshold where one can speak of end-to-end IPv6 connectivity, at least at the service layer.

The document is for a general audience: people who provide or use network services, and people planning IPv6 adoption in an organization. It is informational and does not define a protocol.
sections.eli5: Years ago someone checked who was switching to the new address system. This report checks again to see how far everyone has come.

sections.title: What IPv6-Only Means
sections.content:
"IPv6-only" is only meaningful relative to a scope, so the RFC defines several. An IPv6-only interface forwards only IPv6; a dual-stack interface does not count. An IPv6-only node has only IPv6 addresses on all its interfaces. An IPv6-only service has IPv6 packet headers all the way between the host and the content server.

An IPv6-only overlay means every inner packet header inside the tunnels is IPv6. An IPv6-only underlay means the data plane and control plane are IPv6, though not necessarily the management plane; Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) is given as an example. An IPv6-only network requires every node, including its management plane, to be IPv6-only.

IPv4-as-a-Service (IPv4aaS) provides IPv4 through a transition mechanism (encapsulation or translation over an IPv6-only underlay), so a network can run IPv6-only while users still reach legacy IPv4.
sections.eli5: Being "IPv6-only" can mean a single plug, a whole computer, or a whole network. The report is careful to say which one it means each time.

sections.title: The Global Picture in 2022
sections.content:
The data are mostly as of January 2022. At the end of 2021 the five Regional Internet Registries had 5.2 million available and 12.1 million reserved IPv4 addresses, 17.3 million in total. The RFC notes that address transfers and Network Address Translation (NAT) help absorb demand, with cloud providers appearing to be the most active buyers.

IPv6-capable users grew from 513.07 million in January 2018 to 1,207.61 million in January 2022, which is 29.5% of 4,093.69 million total users. For websites, the share reachable over IPv6 rose from 11.4% to 20.6%. Of the world's top 500 sites, 203 were IPv6 enabled.

The RFC finds no immediate correlation between few IPv4 addresses per person and high IPv6 use. It points instead to regulation and market action, such as a Belgian agreement limiting carrier-grade NAT, a French IPv6 requirement for 5G licensees, and a US plan for 80% of federal IP-capable networks to be IPv6-only by 2025.

These figures are the survey's own snapshot from 2022, not current numbers.
sections.eli5: Counting how many people use the new addresses shows the number growing every year. Some countries moved faster because their governments or companies pushed.

sections.title: Surveys of ISPs, Enterprises and Universities
sections.content:
A survey of European service providers in the third quarter of 2020 found that 79% had IPv6 plans; of those, 60% had activities under way. Dual-Stack was the most adopted approach in wireline (59%) and cellular (39%) networks. The second choices were Dual-Stack Lite (19%) in wireline and 464XLAT (21%) in cellular.

Enterprises lag behind ISPs. In a poll of large North American enterprises in early 2021, almost one third had dual-stacked networks and 20% had portions that were IPv6-only, while 35% had not implemented IPv6 or were stuck at training. None had a fully IPv6 network.

Looking from outside at DNS, mail and website support, the RFC concludes that universities have wider IPv6 support than the other sectors it measured, and that US government support is higher than elsewhere, likely due to a US mandate.
sections.eli5: Internet companies are well on their way. Most other businesses are still learning, because nothing forces them to switch yet.

sections.title: Five Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC describes five scenarios and says they are not necessarily a road map; operators may go in sequence or jump to one.

  • Dual-Stack is the most widely deployed (about 50%). It is cheap to start, but duplicates network resources and still needs IPv4 addresses.
  • IPv6-only overlay carries traffic in IPv6 tunnels and keeps compatibility with IPv4, but is not a long-term solution.
  • IPv6-only underlay keeps the backbone single-protocol; the RFC says Dual-Stack on the transport network is not recommended.
  • IPv4aaS offers IPv4 over an IPv6-only network using methods such as 464XLAT, DS-Lite, lw4o6, MAP-E and MAP-T. RFC 9313 compares them without recommending one.
  • IPv6-only is the final stage: no IPv4 anywhere, even for management.

In June 2021, 108 of 346 World IPv6 Launch operators exceeded 50% IPv6 traffic. The RFC suggests moving to IPv6-only might be reasonable when IPv6 traffic is between 50% and 60%.
sections.eli5: There are several steps from the old addresses to the new ones. You can walk through them one by one or jump ahead, and the last step is to drop the old system entirely.

sections.title: Common Challenges
sections.content:
Choosing a transition method is itself hard, and the best choice differs for fixed operators, mobile operators, enterprises, industrial networks, cloud providers, home equipment and software. Enterprises are shielded from IPv4 depletion by private addressing, so they lack an obvious business case; training and application porting are further hurdles.

On performance, the RFC finds no definitive answer on which IP version is better. The IPv6 failure rate is still a bit worse than IPv4, while the worldwide average latency is slightly in favor of IPv6, and the gaps have been narrowing.

On security, the RFC notes that IPv6-specific protocols such as ICMPv6, the Neighbor Discovery Protocol and Multicast Listener Discovery bring new threats, that extension headers may be dropped in the public Internet, and that IPv4 implementations are generally more robust only because they have been tested longer. The document itself has no IANA actions and no impact on the security of specific protocols.
sections.eli5: Moving is hard for many reasons: people need training, old programs need fixing, and nobody agrees on the best path. But in speed and safety the new system is catching up.
